opus-5.5.text:
I think the part that's still really underdeveloped is permissions, basically, how we decide what an agent is allowed to do, when, and on whose behalf.

Right now most setups are pretty binary. Either you give the agent a tool and it can call it whenever it wants, or you put a human in the loop and approve every single action. Neither of those really scales. If you approve everything, you lose most of the value of having an agent, because you're just babysitting it. And if you approve nothing, you're trusting a probabilistic system with your email, your production database, your credit card, and that's a bit scary.

What's missing is something more like the way we think about permissions for people in an organization. When you hire someone new, you don't hand them the keys to everything on day one, but you also don't make them ask before they send each Slack message. You scope access to the task, you build trust over time, and you have different levels of scrutiny depending on how reversible an action is. Reading a file is very different from deleting one, and drafting an email is very different from sending it to a customer.

So I'd like to see tooling where permissions are task-scoped and context-aware. The agent gets the access it needs for this particular job, it expires when the job is done, and the riskier, harder-to-undo actions get escalated while the routine stuff just flows. Pair that with good audit trails, so you can see after the fact exactly what the agent did and why, and I think you get a lot closer to something people would actually trust in production.

There's also a security angle that I don't think gets enough attention. Once agents are reading untrusted content, like web pages, documents, and emails, and also have tools that act in the world, you open the door to prompt injection being a real attack vector, not just a curiosity. A lot of the defense there has to be at the permission layer rather than hoping the model never gets tricked. So to me, the interesting work isn't just giving agents more tools, it's building the infrastructure around those tools so it's safe to give them more autonomy.

r001.rationale: The response calls agent permissions underdeveloped and proposes task-scoped access with scrutiny based on action risk, but does not identify specifying trust levels for particular tools as the underdeveloped capability.

r002.rationale: It mentions building trust over time, but does not propose making permission prompts depend on the agent’s prior interactions with the user.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most underdeveloped piece is permissions, honestly. Right now the way most agents get access to tools is really binary. You either give the agent the API key or you don't. You either let it call the tool or you don't. And that's a very coarse way to think about it, because the interesting question isn't "can this agent use the browser" or "can this agent run shell commands," it's "under what conditions, with what scope, and with what kind of oversight."

If you think about how we grant permissions to people in an organization, it's much more nuanced than that. A new hire gets read access to a bunch of systems, but they don't get to push to production on day one. They earn trust over time, and the scope of what they're allowed to do expands as they demonstrate they can handle it. We don't really have anything like that for agents yet. There's no good notion of graduated trust, or of permissions that are tied to context, like "you can send emails but only to people already in this thread," or "you can spend money but only up to this amount and only on these vendors."

The other thing that's missing is the feedback loop. When a person does something wrong with a tool, there's usually a review process, there's a log, someone notices and the policy gets adjusted. With agents, the tooling for actually observing what they did with their tool access and then tightening or loosening that access based on what you saw is pretty immature. Most teams I talk to are either so locked down that the agent isn't useful, or they've basically given it the keys and they're hoping for the best.

So I'd say the gap is less about the tools themselves and more about the governance layer around them. Scoped credentials, approval flows that aren't just a human clicking yes on everything, audit trails that are actually designed for agent behavior rather than retrofitted from human-oriented systems. That's where I think a lot of the real work is, and it's not glamorous, but it's what's going to determine whether agents get deployed in settings where the stakes are real.

r001.rationale: The response describes graduated trust and tool permissions that vary by scope and context, identifying trust levels for tool use as underdeveloped.

r002.rationale: It discusses oversight and adjusting permissions based on observed agent behavior, but does not say permission requests should depend on the agent’s prior interactions with the user.

astra-6.text:
I think one underdeveloped area is how we give agents permission to use tools. There’s a big difference between letting an agent read some information and letting it send an email or change something in a production system. But we often treat tool access as a binary decision: either the agent has the tool or it doesn’t.

What I’d like to see is more granular control over what the agent can do, under what circumstances, and when it needs to bring a human into the loop. You might let it investigate an issue autonomously, prepare a proposed change, and then require approval before applying it. The interesting challenge is making those boundaries useful without requiring someone to approve every little step. That’s a pretty important piece of making agents useful in practice.

r001.rationale: It identifies binary tool access as underdeveloped and calls for more granular control over what an agent can do, including different permissions for reading information and changing systems. This communicates tool-specific levels of permission.

r002.rationale: It says permission and human approval should depend on the circumstances and action, but does not tie the decision to the agent’s prior interactions with the user.

sol-6.1.text:
One area that feels underdeveloped is how agents know whether a tool call actually accomplished what they intended. We tend to focus on giving the model access to tools and teaching it how to invoke them. But a successful API response doesn’t necessarily mean the task succeeded.

If an agent changes something in a system, what feedback does it get? Can it inspect the result? Can it recognize that it made the wrong change and recover? I think there’s a lot of room to improve that loop: take an action, observe what happened, and decide whether you’re actually closer to the user’s goal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses checking whether tool calls achieved their intended results, but does not identify specifying trust levels for particular tools as underdeveloped.

r002.rationale: The response discusses observing results and recovery, but does not say permission decisions should depend on prior interactions with the user.
